summary: Describes mailbox referrals for IMAP4, which let a server tell a client that a mailbox actually lives on a different IMAP server. Clients can then follow the pointer without the user noticing. This helps organizations spread mailboxes across several servers while presenting one view of them.

eli5.summary: Imagine asking a librarian for a book and she says it is in the other building, then walks you there. Your email program gets sent to the right computer automatically.

questions: what is an imap mailbox referral
how do imap clients find mailboxes on other servers
how does imap redirect to another server
subtitle: How an IMAP server can point a client to another server that holds a mailbox.

tldr.problem: Organizations may spread mailboxes over several IMAP4 servers, and clients need a way to reach a mailbox that is not on their home server.
tldr.mechanism: The server answers with a tagged NO and a REFERRAL response code holding one or more IMAP URLs, and the client connects to the remote server itself. RLIST and RLSUB list remote mailboxes too.
tldr.outcome: Clients get direct access to distributed mailboxes, which can use bandwidth better than a proxy and does not make the home server impersonate the user.

facts.label: Referral form
facts.value: Tagged NO with a REFERRAL response code

sections.title: Why Mailbox Referrals
sections.content:
With many users, many messages and geographically dispersed IMAP4 servers, it is often desirable to distribute messages among different servers within an organization. An administrator might keep personal mailboxes on a local server and shared mailboxes on a remote one, for example when bandwidth or disk resources make central storage uneconomical.

Mailbox referrals let clients reach such mailboxes seamlessly. The alternative is a proxy method, in which the local server contacts the remote server for the client and relays the data. A referral gives the client a direct connection, which is often a more efficient use of bandwidth and does not require the local server to impersonate the client when authenticating to the remote server.
sections.eli5: Instead of a helper carrying every box between buildings, you are told where to go and fetch it yourself. That is faster for everyone.

sections.title: Terms Used
sections.content:
The RFC defines a few terms. A home server is an IMAP4 server that contains the user's inbox. A remote mailbox is a mailbox not hosted on the home server, and a remote server holds remote mailboxes. A shared mailbox is one that multiple users can access. An IMAP mailbox referral is when the server directs the client to another IMAP mailbox.

Examples use C: and S: for client and server lines. The key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY follow RFC 2119 (RFC 2119).
sections.eli5: Your home server is the place where your mail inbox lives. Any other server that holds some of your boxes is a remote one.

sections.title: How a Referral Works
sections.content:
A server that supports the extension MUST list the keyword MAILBOX-REFERRALS in its CAPABILITY response. The client needs to do nothing to turn it on, and the server MUST NOT return referrals that result in a loop.

A referral is a tagged NO response with a REFERRAL response code. The code carries one or more URLs separated by spaces, as defined in RFC 1738. Multiple URLs for one object MUST all be of the same type, and for this purpose they are IMAP URLs from RFC 2192. A client MUST be prepared for a URL of any type but needs to process only IMAP URLs.

A server MAY give several referrals if there are several replicas of the mailbox, which allows load balancing or failover. How replicas are kept in sync is not covered. The preferred URL SHOULD be first, with the rest in descending order of preference. Clients may face synchronization issues if the UIDVALIDITY of the referred mailboxes differs.

Example: A001 NO [REFERRAL IMAP://user;AUTH=*@SERVER2/REMOTE]Remote Mailbox. The user;AUTH=* form is required by RFC 2192 to avoid a client falling back to anonymous login.
sections.eli5: The server says no, but adds a note with one or more addresses of where the box really is. If there are copies, the best address comes first.

sections.title: Referrals for Each Command
sections.content:
A server MAY answer SELECT, EXAMINE, DELETE, SUBSCRIBE, UNSUBSCRIBE, STATUS or APPEND with one or more referrals. The client then opens a new connection, or reuses an existing one, to the remote server and issues the commands there. In the RFC's examples the client authenticates again on the second connection, then closes it with LOGOUT and continues with its first connection.

For CREATE, the server MAY refer the client to another server, choosing by any means such as the mailbox name hierarchy. Alternatively, because the home server must keep a list of referred remote mailboxes, it MAY accept the CREATE and answer with referrals on later commands.

For RENAME, the server MAY return pairs of referrals: the existing mailbox and the requested new name. If the two are on different servers, they cannot perform the rename, and the client MAY use CREATE, FETCH, APPEND and DELETE on both servers. If both are on the same server, the client can simply reissue RENAME there.

For COPY, a referral means the destination mailbox is remote. The client MAY use FETCH and APPEND against both servers to get the same result.
sections.eli5: Most things you do to a box can send you to another computer. For moving a box between two computers, your email program has to fetch the mail from one and store it on the other.

sections.title: RLIST and RLSUB
sections.content:
Remote mailboxes reachable only by referral SHOULD NOT appear in LIST and LSUB responses from the home server. They MUST appear in RLIST and RLSUB responses. A referral-capable client issues RLIST and RLSUB in place of LIST and LSUB, which avoids showing inaccessible remote mailboxes to clients that do not support referrals.

Both commands take a reference name and a mailbox name with possible wildcards. They behave like LIST and LSUB, except that remote mailboxes are returned along with local ones. The results are OK, NO or BAD, and the untagged responses are LIST and LSUB. Hierarchy referrals, where a client must connect to the remote server to list the children of a mailbox, are not addressed.

Mailboxes on the home server need not exist on the remote server. Extra mailboxes on the remote server are not reachable by referral unless the RLIST against the home server lists them.
sections.eli5: Referral-aware programs ask for the long list, which includes boxes kept elsewhere. Older programs get the short list so they never see boxes they cannot open.

sections.title: Formal Syntax
sections.content: The syntax uses ABNF. A mailbox_referral is a tag, a space, NO, a referral response code, and then text. The referral_response_code is [, REFERRAL and one or more space-prefixed URLs, then ]. The commands rlist and rlsub are the command name followed by a mailbox and a list_mailbox, both as defined in RFC 2060 (RFC 2060).
sections.eli5: The grammar is a strict recipe: the word REFERRAL, then addresses in square brackets, so programs can read it without guessing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Referrals use IMAP URLs, so they carry the same security considerations as general URLs (RFC 1738) and IMAP URLs (RFC 2192).

With this capability it is potentially easier to write a rogue server that injects a bogus referral and sends a user to the wrong mailbox. The RFC notes that although referrals lower the effort needed to write such a server, the referral response also makes the intrusion easier to detect.
sections.eli5: A fake server could send you to the wrong place. But because it has to say so openly, it is also easier to catch.
